description: Radium is a chemical element with symbol Ra and atomic number 88, the sixth element in group 2 of the periodic table known as the alkaline earth metals. It is the heaviest known alkaline earth metal and the only radioactive member of its group. Pure radium is a volatile, lustrous silvery-white metal that readily reacts with nitrogen upon exposure to air, forming a black surface layer of radium nitride.
uses: Radium was widely used in self-luminous paints following its discovery due to its property of emitting ionizing radiation that can excite fluorescent chemicals and cause radioluminescence. From the 1910s to the 1970s, it was used as a radioactive source for radioluminescent devices and in radioactive quackery for its supposed curative power. As of 2018, other than in nuclear medicine and the production of actinium in nuclear reactors, radium has no commercial applications, having been replaced with less dangerous radioisotopes in nearly all its applications.
characteristics: All isotopes of radium are radioactive, with radium-226 being the most stable with a half-life of 1,600 years. Radium has a melting point of either 700°C or 960°C and a boiling point of 1,737°C, with a density of 5.5 g/cm³. It crystallizes in a body-centered cubic structure and is considered particularly toxic and carcinogenic due to its radioactivity and its tendency to accumulate in bones by mimicking calcium.
